figures.name: Ambrose of Milan
figures.dates: born c. 339-340 at Trier; bishop of Milan from 374; died 4 April 397 at Milan
figures.places: Trier (born in the governor's residence), Rome (raised), Sirmium, Milan (governor of Liguria and Aemilia, then bishop); embassies to the usurper Maximus at Trier
figures.role: Roman provincial governor made bishop of Milan by popular acclaim while still unbaptized; preacher, hymn-writer, adviser and opponent of emperors; the man who baptized Augustine
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Anglican churches and honoured by Lutherans; one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church (feast 7 December). Cautions a reader should know: (1) in 388 he pressed Theodosius to drop the order that a bishop at Callinicum rebuild a synagogue his people had burned, and wrote "I declare that I set fire to the synagogue, or at least that I ordered those who did it" (Letter 40); his language about Jews there is hostile, and almost no one today would defend his stand. (2) He fought to keep the pagan Altar of Victory out of the Senate, so his pleas for freedom of conscience (Letter 21) were made for his own side. (3) Much is wrongly credited to him: the Te Deum, most of the hymns called "Ambrosian" (only a handful are certainly his), and the Pauline commentaries now called "Ambrosiaster". (4) Our Life of him is by his secretary Paulinus, written about 422 at Augustine's request: close to him, but a devoted admirer who includes miracles.
figures.hook: He walked into Milan's cathedral as the Roman governor to calm a riot over the choice of a bishop, a child's voice cried "Ambrose Bishop", he fled the city at midnight to escape it, and eight days after his baptism he was bishop anyway.

stories.story: As a baby asleep in his cradle in the governor's courtyard, a swarm of bees covered his face and went in and out of his mouth. His father stopped the nurse from driving them off, watched them fly up out of sight, and said: "If this little child shall live he shall be something great." Paulinus reads the bees as a sign of his honeyed words.
stories.source: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose, section 3

stories.story: Sent to Milan as governor, he went to the church to stop a riot between Arians and Catholics over a new bishop. A child's voice cried "Ambrose Bishop," and the whole crowd took it up. To put them off he ordered tortures from the bench, tried to declare himself a philosopher, and even had prostitutes come to his house publicly. Then he fled at midnight toward Pavia, got lost, and was found at dawn at Milan's own Roman Gate. He hid on a nobleman's estate until the man gave him up. Baptized by a Catholic bishop at his own insistence, he was ordained bishop eight days later.
stories.source: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose, sections 6-9

stories.story: Augustine, then an unbelieving teacher of rhetoric, could hardly get a word with him for the crowds. When Ambrose had a spare moment he read, and he read silently: "his eyes glanced over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were silent." Visitors would sit a long time in silence and then leave rather than interrupt him.
stories.source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 6, chapter 3, section 3

stories.story: In Holy Week of 386 the boy-emperor Valentinian II and his Arian mother Justina ordered him to hand over a church. He refused, and his people locked themselves in the basilica with him for days while soldiers surrounded it. To keep their spirits up, hymns and psalms were sung "after the manner of the Eastern Church", a custom Augustine says was then copied by almost all congregations. Ambrose told his flock: "my tears are my weapons, for these are a priest's defense."
stories.source: Sermon against Auxentius, sections 1-2 and 34; Augustine, Confessions, Book 9, chapter 7, section 15

stories.story: After the emperor Theodosius's soldiers massacred many innocent people at Thessalonica in 390, Ambrose did not denounce him in public. He wrote him a private letter in his own hand, "which you alone may read", saying he dared not celebrate the Eucharist in his presence until he repented as King David had. When Theodosius pleaded that David too had sinned, Paulinus records the reply: "You who have followed him as he sinned, follow him as he corrected himself." The emperor did public penance.
stories.source: Letter 51, sections 5, 7, 13-14; Paulinus, Life of Ambrose, section 24

stories.story: He broke up the church's sacred vessels and sold the metal to buy back people captured by the Goths, and was attacked for it. His answer: "it was far better to preserve souls than gold for the Lord."
stories.source: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 2, chapter 28, sections 136-137

stories.story: Monica, Augustine's mother, was upset to find that Milan did not fast on Saturdays as Rome did. Augustine asked Ambrose what she should do. He answered: "When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast." Augustine said he held that answer ever after as if it came from heaven. It is the root of the saying "When in Rome, do as the Romans do."
stories.source: Augustine, Letter 54 (to Januarius), chapter 2, section 3; also Letter 36, section 32

stories.story: Dying in 397, he was begged by Milan's leading men to pray for a longer life. He answered: "I have not so lived among you that I am ashamed to live nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord!"
stories.source: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose, section 45

temperament.trait: Firm with power but not rebellious
temperament.evidence: "You yourselves know that I am wont to show respect to our emperors, but not to yield to them, to offer myself freely to punishment, and not to fear what is prepared for me."

temperament.trait: Wept with sinners and kept their secrets
temperament.evidence: His secretary says that whenever anyone confessed to him, "he so wept that he compelled that one to weep", and that he told the crimes confessed to him "to no one except to the Lord alone".
temperament.source: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose, section 39

temperament.evidence: Augustine on arriving in Milan: "That man of God received me like a father, and looked with a benevolent and episcopal kindliness on my change of abode."

Augustine could seldom speak to him, "debarred from hearing and speaking to him by crowds of busy people, whose infirmities he devoted himself to"; his few free minutes went to silent reading, and "who dared interrupt one so intent?"
To Theodosius: "This vehemence of yours I preferred to commend privately to your own consideration, rather than possibly raise it by any action of mine in public."
"I think we ought to avoid not only broad jokes, but all kinds of jests, unless perchance it is not unfitting at the time for our conversation to be agreeable and pleasant."
temperament.source: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 23, section 103

genuine_lines.quote: For the Emperor is within the Church, not above it.
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The palaces belong to the Emperor, the churches to the Bishop.
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: against weapons, soldiers, Goths, my tears are my weapons, for these are a priest's defense.
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Beasts do not drive out beasts, yet man shuts out man.
genuine_lines.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out, and to spend on those who need.
genuine_lines.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: You cover your walls, you strip men naked.
genuine_lines.translation: Martin R. P. McGuire, S. Ambrosii De Nabuthae, Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 15 (1927)

genuine_lines.quote: Now no one can repent to good purpose unless he hopes for mercy.
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: For rebukes are good, and often better than a silent friendship.
genuine_lines.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Not all weeping proceeds from unbelief or weakness.
genuine_lines.work: On the Death of his Brother Satyrus
genuine_lines.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: I have not so lived among you that I am ashamed to live nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord!
genuine_lines.work: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose (his dying words, reported by his secretary)
genuine_lines.translation: Mary Simplicia Kaniecka, Vita Sancti Ambrosii, Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 16 (1928)

misattributed.line: "When in Rome, do as the Romans do."
misattributed.truth: The proverb in that wording is medieval and later. What Ambrose actually said, as Augustine reports it, was about fasting: "When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast" (Augustine, Letter 54.3 and Letter 36.32).

misattributed.line: The Te Deum ("We praise Thee, O God") was composed by Ambrose and Augustine, singing alternate verses at Augustine's baptism.
misattributed.truth: A legend from a later chronicle falsely ascribed to Dacius of Milan. No early source says it; many scholars credit the hymn to Nicetas of Remesiana or leave it anonymous.

misattributed.line: "Every truth, by whomever it is spoken, is from the Holy Spirit."
misattributed.truth: Often cited as Ambrose (Aquinas quotes it under his name), but it comes from the commentary on 1 Corinthians 12:3 by the anonymous author scholars call "Ambrosiaster", whose works circulated under Ambrose's name.

misattributed.line: Ambrose met Theodosius at the church door, laid his hand on him and refused him entry with a long speech.
misattributed.truth: That dramatic scene with its speeches is Theodoret's (Church History 5.17-18, written about 450). Ambrose's own account is a private letter (Letter 51), and his secretary Paulinus says only that he refused the emperor access to the church until he did public penance (Life 24).

misattributed.line: Ambrose wrote the whole body of "Ambrosian" hymns.
misattributed.truth: Only a few are securely his, chiefly those Augustine quotes as his (Deus creator omnium, Aeterne rerum conditor, Iam surgit hora tertia, Intende qui regis Israel). The rest are later imitations in his style.

opinions.position: Learn to keep quiet before you learn to speak. Far more people sin by talking than by staying silent, and keeping silent is the harder skill.
opinions.side_note: Side: for silence as a discipline (his book on duties opens with it).
opinions.quote: How many have I seen to fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely one by keeping silent; and so it is more difficult to know how to keep silent than how to speak.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle ("think before you speak"), so as a bare claim it is one-sided. It splits better if sharpened: talkative, expressive people and those who value speaking up would resist the idea that silence is usually the safer choice.

opinions.position: Giving to the poor is not charity but paying back a debt. The earth was made for everyone, so what the rich keep for themselves partly belongs to the poor.
opinions.side_note: Side: strongly against private wealth as an absolute right.
opinions.quote: Not from your own do you bestow upon the poor man, but you make return from what is his. For what has been given as common for the use of all, you appropriate to yourself alone. The earth belongs to all, not to the rich
opinions.translation: Martin R. P. McGuire, S. Ambrosii De Nabuthae, Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 15 (1927)
opinions.today: Sharply split, and politically charged: many on the left and many Catholics (it is quoted in modern papal teaching) agree; many conservatives and libertarians hold that what you earn is yours and giving is generosity, not a debt.

opinions.position: Spending on your own grand house while people go without is a scandal: the rich decorate walls and stable horses in gold while the poor ask for bread.
opinions.side_note: Side: against luxury while others lack.
opinions.quote: The poor man seeks money and has it not; a man asks for bread, and your horse champs gold under his teeth.
opinions.translation: Martin R. P. McGuire, S. Ambrosii De Nabuthae, Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 15 (1927)
opinions.today: Most people agree with the image but disagree about whether owning nice things while others are poor is actually wrong. Split on the practical claim.

opinions.position: Holy objects are worth less than people. He melted down the church's consecrated vessels to ransom captives and defended it: the Church has gold to spend on the needy, not to guard.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with Jerome ("the true temple of Christ is the believer's soul"). Opposite: those who keep churches beautiful and treasures intact as offerings to God.
opinions.quote: we have followed it up among the people so as to confess and to add again and again that it was far better to preserve souls than gold for the Lord.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many would sell church treasures to feed people; others (and many who love old churches, art and heritage) say beautiful things offered to God should be kept. A good quiz claim: "If my church owned valuable treasures, I'd sell them to help the poor."

opinions.position: A Christian should not kill even an armed robber to save his own life, and should not save himself at another's cost (not even grabbing the one plank in a shipwreck).
opinions.side_note: He held this alongside a duty to defend others (see next item). Augustine later took the same line on private self-defense.
opinions.quote: I do not think that a Christian, a just and a wise man, ought to save his own life by the death of another; just as when he meets with an armed robber he cannot return his blows, lest in defending his life he should stain his love toward his neighbour.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly one-sided against him today: most people, Christians included, think self-defense is plainly allowed. A minority of Christian pacifists (Mennonites, some Catholics and Orthodox) agree with him. Useful precisely because it surprises.

opinions.position: Courage means driving harm away from others. If you can protect a friend from harm and do not, you are as guilty as the one who harms him.
opinions.side_note: The other half of his view: no violence to save yourself, but a duty to protect others (Moses defending the Hebrew).
opinions.quote: He who does not keep harm off a friend, if he can, is as much in fault as he who causes it.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree you should help, but "as guilty as the attacker" splits people: many say doing wrong is worse than failing to stop it.

opinions.position: Courage in war that protects your country from invaders, or defends the weak at home, is full of justice.
opinions.side_note: Side: war can be just. Against Martin of Tours, who refused to fight.
opinions.quote: For courage, which in war preserves one's country from the barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or comrades from robbers, is full of justice
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people accept defensive war; Christian pacifists do not. Pairs well with Martin for a nearest/farthest split.

opinions.position: A Christian judge may lawfully sentence a criminal to death, but it is better not to. Mercy leaves room for the guilty to repent.
opinions.side_note: Replying to a Christian judge named Studius. He also notes some Christians refused communion to judges who had passed death sentences, and he would not go that far.
opinions.quote: You see therefore both what power your commission gives you, and also whither mercy would lead you; you will be excused if you do it, and praised if you do it not.
opinions.translation: Letters of S. Ambrose, Library of the Fathers (Oxford: James Parker, 1881), transcribed by Roger Pearse
opinions.today: Split. In the US many Christians support the death penalty; the Catholic Church now opposes it, and most of Europe has abolished it. His middle position (allowed, but mercy is better) is itself a distinct answer.

opinions.position: The emperor is a son of the Church, inside it and under its moral authority, not above it. Churches belong to God, not to Caesar.
opinions.side_note: Side: the Church is independent of the state and can judge rulers.
opinions.quote: For what is more full of respect than that the Emperor should be called the son of the Church. As it is said, it is said without sin, since it is said with the divine favour. For the Emperor is within the Church, not above it.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split along church-state lines: many believers want faith to hold leaders to account; secular people (and many Christians) want religion kept out of government altogether.

opinions.position: Laws cannot make anyone believe; they can only frighten the timid into going along.
opinions.side_note: Written against an imperial law forcing Arian worship. Caution: he did not apply the same freedom to pagans (Altar of Victory) or to Jews (Callinicum).
opinions.quote: The law of God has taught us what we should follow, human laws cannot teach us this. They can compel a change in the timid, but they cannot inspire faith.
opinions.translation: Letters of S. Ambrose, Library of the Fathers (Oxford: James Parker, 1881), transcribed by Roger Pearse
opinions.today: Almost everyone agrees today that faith cannot be forced, so it is one-sided as a bare claim.

opinions.position: He argued that a Christian emperor must not make Christians rebuild a synagogue their bishop had had burned, and offered to take the blame himself.
opinions.side_note: Caution: include only with care. It shows his zeal at its worst and sits against his plea that faith cannot be forced.
opinions.quote: I declare that I set fire to the synagogue, or at least that I ordered those who did it, that there might not be a place where Christ was denied.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Overwhelmingly rejected today, by Christians too. One-sided, so it is no use as a quiz statement, but a reader should know it.

opinions.position: If a friend is doing wrong, rebuke him, first in private and then openly if he will not listen, even if it hurts him. An honest rebuke is better than a friendship that stays silent.
opinions.side_note: Side: for correcting others directly.
opinions.quote: one ought to rebuke him secretly — if he does not listen, one must do it openly. For rebukes are good, and often better than a silent friendship. Even if a friend thinks himself hurt, still rebuke him
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split. Many people today think it is not their place to criticise a friend's choices ("live and let live"); others value blunt honesty between friends.

opinions.position: Friendship never outranks honesty. If God's cause or your country's good requires it, you must give true witness against a friend.
opinions.side_note: He adds that it must be true witness and done with caution. The Roman philosophers had debated whether one should betray one's country for a friend.
opinions.quote: For what if the cause of God or of one's country compels one to give witness? Ought friendship to take a higher place than our religion, or our love for our fellow citizens?
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Genuinely split. Many people say they would never turn in a close friend or family member; others put truth and the law first. A strong quiz claim: "I would testify against a close friend if he had done something seriously wrong."

opinions.topic: new: standing up to the powerful
opinions.position: Respect rulers, but do not give way to them when they are wrong. He barred the emperor from the Eucharist until he repented of a massacre.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with Martin of Tours, who refused the usurper's table and passed the emperor's cup to his own priest.
opinions.quote: I, I say, have no cause for a charge of contumacy against you, but have cause for fear; I dare not offer the sacrifice if you intend to be present.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people admire it in principle; they split over whether church leaders should confront politicians publicly (for example, over communion).

opinions.position: Refusing forgiveness to people who have fallen badly is pride and cruelty. Without hope of mercy, no one can truly repent.
opinions.side_note: Side: for second chances (written against the Novatianists, who refused to readmit grave sinners).
opinions.quote: For what is more harsh than to inflict a penance which they do not relax, and by refusing pardon to take away the incentive to penance and repentance? Now no one can repent to good purpose unless he hopes for mercy.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree in the abstract; they split over particular cases (abusers, public figures).

opinions.position: Real repentance is rare and costly. He found it easier to find people who had never fallen than people who had truly repented, because true penitence means giving up honours, drink and comfort.
opinions.side_note: His hard edge inside the merciful view: pardon is open, but repentance must be real.
opinions.quote: But I have more easily found such as had preserved their innocence than such as had fittingly repented.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many people are sceptical of quick public apologies and would agree; others think insisting on proof of change is unforgiving.

opinions.position: Weeping for the dead is not a lack of faith. Natural grief is one thing, despairing sadness another.
opinions.side_note: Side: tears are allowed (spoken at his brother Satyrus's funeral). Against Jerome's rebuke to Paula.
opinions.quote: Not all weeping proceeds from unbelief or weakness. Natural grief is one thing, distrustful sadness is another, and there is a very great difference between longing for what you have lost and lamenting that you have lost it.
opinions.work: On the Death of his Brother Satyrus
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Nearly everyone agrees today that grief is healthy, so it is one-sided; useful only against Jerome's harsher letter.

opinions.position: Anger itself is natural and sometimes right: there are wrongs one ought to be angry at, and never being angry would be apathy. The task is to govern it by reason.
opinions.side_note: Side: for right anger, not for stamping it out.
opinions.quote: Be angry where there is a fault against which you ought to be angry. For it is impossible not to be roused up by the baseness of many things; otherwise we might be accounted, not virtuous, but apathetic and neglectful.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today agree that anger at injustice is healthy; those drawn to calm, Stoic or Buddhist ideals would disagree.

opinions.position: Serious people should avoid joking, not only crude jokes but jesting generally, except for pleasant conversation at the right moment.
opinions.side_note: Side: against much humour. Written for clergy.
opinions.quote: Do we seek for something to laugh at, that laughing here we may weep hereafter? I think we ought to avoid not only broad jokes, but all kinds of jests, unless perchance it is not unfitting at the time for our conversation to be agreeable and pleasant.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly one-sided against him: almost everyone today values humour. Only useful as a surprising reveal.

opinions.position: Dancing at parties and weddings is dangerous for modesty; he quotes the pagan saying that no one dances sober unless he is mad, and recalls that John the Baptist died at a dancer's wish.
opinions.side_note: He did praise David's dancing before the ark as spiritual (Letter 58), so his target is party dancing.
opinions.quote: For as a certain teacher of this world has said: No one dances when sober unless he is mad.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly one-sided against him today, though some conservative churches still discourage social dancing.

opinions.position: Singing hymns together is powerful and good: it turns a whole congregation into teachers of the faith. He admitted his hymns had captivated the people and was glad of it.
opinions.side_note: Side: for music in worship. Against Jerome's advice that a girl be "deaf to the sound of the organ".
opinions.quote: They declare also that the people have been led astray by the strains of my hymns. I certainly do not deny it. That is a lofty strain, and there is nothing more powerful than it.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly agreed today. Splits a little on style: some want only simple congregational song, others choirs or bands.

opinions.position: On practices that vary from place to place and do not touch faith or morals, follow the custom of wherever you are, so you neither give offence nor take it.
opinions.side_note: The origin of "When in Rome". Reported by Augustine, who asked him the question for Monica.
opinions.quote: When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast. On the same principle, do you observe the custom prevailing in whatever Church you come to, if you desire neither to give offense by your conduct, nor to find cause of offense in another's.
opinions.work: Augustine, Letter 54 (to Januarius), reporting Ambrose's words
opinions.translation: J.G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 1st series, vol. 1 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people adapt to local ways when travelling or visiting another church; others keep their own convictions and practices wherever they go. A good quiz claim: "When I'm somewhere new, I follow the way things are done there."

opinions.position: It is cruel to drive foreigners out of a city in a famine, just when they most need help. Even animals do not do that to their own kind.
opinions.side_note: He praises a Christian prefect of Rome who raised money to feed the city instead of expelling outsiders.
opinions.quote: But they, too, who would forbid the city to strangers cannot have our approval. They would expel them at the very time when they ought to help
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Sharply split today on immigration: many say a country must look after its own first in a crisis; others say that is exactly when to help outsiders.

opinions.position: Old ways are not right just because they are old. Everything in creation has moved toward something better, and there is no shame in changing for the better.
opinions.side_note: Written against Symmachus's plea to keep the ancestral pagan rites. Ambrose here is the one arguing for the new.
opinions.quote: But, he says, the rites of our ancestors ought to be retained. But what, seeing that all things have made progress towards what is better?
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: progressives and traditionalists answer this very differently. Neat irony for readers: here the Church Father argues for change against the defenders of tradition.

opinions.position: Where faith is required, stop arguing. Clever debate wins nothing; simple believers grow while subtle disputers lose their followers.
opinions.side_note: Side: faith over argument. He himself argued at length, and Augustine found his reasoning decisive.
opinions.quote: Away with arguments, where faith is required; now let dialectic hold her peace, even in the midst of her schools.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many believers value simple trust; many others, Christian and not, think faith should be questioned and argued out.

opinions.position: He did not want the office and ran from it; once made bishop he said he had to learn and teach at the same time.
opinions.side_note: Side: reluctant office-holder.
opinions.quote: For I was carried off from the judgment seat, and the garb [infulis] of office, to enter on the priesthood, and began to teach you, what I myself had not yet learned.
opinions.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many admire reluctance to take power; others say if you are able you should step up. Moderate split.

opinions.position: When threatened, he would not flee and leave his people, but neither would he fight: he would stay, grieve and accept whatever came.
opinions.side_note: Side: stay, and resist without force.
opinions.quote: I ought not, I cannot resist in any other way; but to fly and forsake the Church is not my way; lest any one should suppose I did so from fear of some heavier punishment.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most admire standing firm; many would also say it is sensible to leave when in danger.

opinions.position: A young woman called to consecrated virginity should hold out against her parents' pleading; winning that fight at home is the first victory.
opinions.side_note: Side: calling over family wishes (though he urges her to win them by patience, not defiance).
opinions.quote: And the anxious entreaties of your parents are your first battles. Conquer your affection first, O maiden. If you conquer your home, you conquer the world.
opinions.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 10 (1896), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many people today say follow your own path even against parents; many families and cultures put parents' wishes first.

opinions.topic: new: being seen as too religious
opinions.position: It is shameful that people are embarrassed to look too devoted to their faith, while no one blushes at pagan rites. He defended a rich senator (Paulinus of Nola) who gave everything away, against the mockery of high society.
opinions.side_note: Useful new claim about public devotion and caring what others think.
opinions.quote: Truly I grieve that, while falsehood is so respected, there should be such negligence as regards the Truth, that many are ashamed of seeming too devoted to our holy religion
opinions.translation: Letters of S. Ambrose, Library of the Fathers (Oxford: James Parker, 1881), transcribed by Roger Pearse
opinions.today: Split: many Christians today keep faith private and would be uneasy looking "too religious"; others think faith should be visible and unashamed.

opinions.position: Much of the Old Testament must be read spiritually, not only by the letter; he often preached "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life".
opinions.side_note: Side: for spiritual or allegorical reading. His method is what won Augustine over.
opinions.quote: with delight I heard Ambrose, in his sermons to the people, oftentimes most diligently recommend this text as a rule —The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life; while, drawing aside the mystic veil, he spiritually laid open that which, accepted according to the letter, seemed to teach perverse doctrines
opinions.translation: J.G. Pilkington, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 1st series, vol. 1 (1886), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split among Christians: many evangelicals prefer the plain, literal sense; Catholics, Orthodox and many mainline readers accept spiritual senses.

opinions.position: He told the sins people confessed to him to no one but God, so that a bishop would be an intercessor for sinners, not their accuser.
opinions.side_note: Reported by his secretary. Practice rather than a written rule.
opinions.quote: cases of crime, however, which anyone confessed to him, he told to no one except to the Lord alone with whom he pleaded, leaving a good example to future bishops that they should be intercessors before God rather than accusers before men.
opinions.work: Paulinus of Milan, Life of Ambrose
opinions.translation: Mary Simplicia Kaniecka, Vita Sancti Ambrosii, Catholic University of America Patristic Studies 16 (1928)
opinions.today: Live dispute today: the confessional seal versus laws requiring clergy to report crimes such as child abuse. Sharply split.

sparring.over: Ambrose's book On the Holy Spirit. Jerome, without naming him, called its author a jackdaw decked in another bird's feathers and the book "flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty", mere Latin copied from good Greek. Rufinus identified the target and defended Ambrose.
sparring.source: Jerome's preface to his translation of Didymus On the Holy Spirit, quoted in Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2, sections 24-25

sparring.with: Auxentius of Milan (Arian bishop) and the Empress Justina
sparring.over: Handing a Milan basilica to the Arians in 385-386; Ambrose refused, and his people occupied the church with him.
Callinicum (388): Ambrose made him drop the order to rebuild a burned synagogue. Thessalonica (390): Ambrose barred him from the Eucharist until he repented of the massacre.

sparring.with: Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus (Arian bishops)
sparring.over: The divinity of Christ; Ambrose led their condemnation at the Council of Aquileia in 381.
sparring.source: Acts of the Council of Aquileia (in Ambrose's letters, Letters 9-12 in the Benedictine order)

sparring.over: Whether virginity and fasting earn any higher reward than marriage and eating with thanks. Ambrose's synod at Milan condemned him in 393.
Seeking the death of heretics. On his embassy to Maximus at Trier he refused communion with bishops "who sought the death of any one, even though they were heretics", and was expelled from the court.
Whether the Church may forgive grave sins committed after baptism.
