figures.name: Jerome
figures.dates: born c. 347 at Stridon (on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia); died 30 September 419 or 420 at Bethlehem
figures.places: Stridon; Rome (student, later secretary to Pope Damasus, 382-385); Trier and Aquileia; the Syrian desert of Chalcis (hermit, c. 375-377); Antioch; Constantinople (studied under Gregory of Nazianzus); Bethlehem (monastery with Paula, 386 until death)
figures.role: Priest, monk and scholar; translator of most of the Latin Bible (the Vulgate) from Hebrew and Greek; commentator, historian of Christian writers, and author of about 125 surviving letters, many of them furious
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Anglican churches and honoured by Lutherans; one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church (feast 30 September in the West, 15 June in the East). Cautions: (1) he was savage in controversy and did not always argue fairly; he admitted as much (Letter 48.13) and broke publicly with his oldest friend, Rufinus. (2) His writing on marriage and women is often extreme; even his friend Pammachius tried to keep Against Jovinian from circulating in Rome because it seemed to belittle marriage. (3) He left Rome in 385 under a cloud: after the death of the young widow Blaesilla, blamed on fasting, crowds turned on the monks, and there was gossip about his friendship with her mother Paula, which he denied (Letters 39 and 45). (4) He began as an admirer and translator of Origen and later attacked Origenism fiercely. (5) Not all of the Vulgate is his: he revised the Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew, but the rest of the New Testament was revised by others. (6) He was never a cardinal, and his lion is a borrowed legend.
figures.hook: Feverish in the desert, he dreamed he stood before Christ's judgment seat and heard "You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ", was flogged, and woke, he swore, with bruised shoulders: the man who then gave the West its Latin Bible also wrote some of the angriest letters in Christian history.

stories.story: Close to death from fever, he dreamed he was dragged before the Judge. Asked who he was, he said "I am a Christian" and was told: "You lie. You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ." He was whipped and swore never again to own or read pagan books. He insisted it was no ordinary dream: "my shoulders were black and blue". Years later, when Rufinus accused him of perjury for still quoting the classics, Jerome answered that it had been "a promise for the future, not the abolition of my memory of the past".
stories.source: Letter 22 (to Eustochium), section 30; Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 30

stories.story: Alone in the Syrian desert, burnt black by the sun and starving himself, he still found his mind full of "bevies of girls" and the pleasures of Rome. To tame his thoughts he asked a converted Jew to teach him Hebrew, and after the elegance of Cicero and Pliny he began to learn "words both harsh and guttural". That hard-won Hebrew later made the Vulgate possible.
stories.source: Letter 22, section 7; Letter 125 (to Rusticus), section 12

stories.story: When Blaesilla, a young widow he had guided into strict fasting, died in Rome in 384, her mother Paula collapsed at the funeral and the crowd muttered: "How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why do we not stone them or hurl them into the Tiber?" Within a year Jerome left Rome, writing bitterly on the ship: "I am said to be an infamous turncoat, a slippery knave, one who lies and deceives others by Satanic arts."
stories.source: Letter 39 (to Paula), section 6; Letter 45 (to Asella), section 2

stories.story: His new translation of Jonah called the plant that shaded the prophet an "ivy" instead of the familiar "gourd". When a bishop at Oea in North Africa read it out, the congregation rioted and the bishop nearly lost his church. Augustine wrote to warn him; Jerome replied that the old complaint about the gourd had been answered long ago.
stories.source: Augustine, Letter 71 (Jerome's Letter 104), section 5; Jerome to Augustine, Letter 112 (Augustine's Letter 75), section 22

stories.story: When the younger Augustine questioned his commentary on Galatians, Jerome, by then old, told him to pick on someone his own age: "desist from annoying an old man, who seeks retirement in his monastic cell", and reminded him of the boxing match in Virgil where the old champion beats the young one: "The tired ox treads with a firmer step." Their later letters were warm.
stories.source: Letter 105 (Augustine's Letter 72), section 3; Letter 102 (Augustine's Letter 68), section 2

stories.story: In 410 the news reached Bethlehem that Alaric's Goths had taken Rome. Jerome, dictating a letter about his friend Marcella, who had been beaten by the invaders and died soon after, broke down: "My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken".
stories.source: Letter 127 (to Principia), section 12

stories.story: A visitor from Gaul, Postumianus, stayed six months with him at Bethlehem and reported that he was always reading or writing, day and night, and at war with everyone: "The heretics hate him, because he never desists from attacking them; the clerics hate him, because he assails their life and crimes."
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues, Book 1, chapters 8-9

temperament.evidence: "I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions."

temperament.trait: Hated and loved in equal measure (a witness)
temperament.evidence: Postumianus: "The heretics hate him, because he never desists from attacking them; the clerics hate him, because he assails their life and crimes. But beyond doubt, all the good admire and love him".
"He is always occupied in reading, always at his books with his whole heart: he takes no rest day or night; he is perpetually either reading or writing something."

temperament.trait: Hard on himself, honest about temptation
temperament.evidence: "I used to dread my very cell as though it knew my thoughts; and, stern and angry with myself, I used to make my way alone into the desert."
He renamed Vigilantius ("Wakeful") "Dormitantius" ("Sleepy"): "All at once Vigilantius, or, more correctly, Dormitantius, has arisen".

temperament.trait: Tender in grief, despite his own rules
temperament.evidence: On the death of young Nepotian: "As often as I try to express myself in words and to scatter the flowers of this encomium upon his tomb, my eyes fill with tears, my grief returns, and I can think of nothing but his death."

genuine_lines.quote: You lie. You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.
genuine_lines.work: Letter 22 (to Eustochium), the words spoken to him in his dream
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The friendship which can cease has never been real.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The face is the mirror of the mind and a woman's eyes without a word betray the secrets of her heart.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Always have some work on hand, that the devil may find you busy.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: When the stomach is full, it is easy to talk of fasting.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Of two imperfect things holy rusticity is better than sinful eloquence.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: If you ask for authority, the world outweighs its capital.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: But I thank the Lord that from this seed of learning sown in bitterness I now cull sweet fruits.
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
genuine_lines.location: Prologue to Book 1 (Latin: "ignoratio Scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est")
genuine_lines.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin (Migne, PL 24)

genuine_lines.quote: The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken
genuine_lines.work: Letter 127 (to Principia), on the sack of Rome
genuine_lines.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: Jerome pulled a thorn from a lion's paw and the lion lived with him in the monastery.
misattributed.truth: The story is told of Abba Gerasimus of the Jordan in John Moschus's Spiritual Meadow (early 7th century). Later Latin writers moved it to Jerome, perhaps because Gerasimus and Hieronymus sounded alike. Nothing in Jerome or his contemporaries mentions it.

misattributed.line: Jerome the cardinal (the red hat and robes in paintings).
misattributed.truth: An anachronism: there were no cardinals in the modern sense in his day. He served as secretary to Pope Damasus, which later artists turned into a cardinal's rank.

misattributed.line: "Good, better, best. Never let it rest, till your good is better and your better is best."
misattributed.truth: Widely credited to St Jerome online, but no source in his works; it is a modern schoolroom rhyme.

misattributed.line: Jerome alone translated the whole Latin Vulgate from the originals.
misattributed.truth: Only in part. He revised the Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew; the rest of the New Testament in the Vulgate was revised by others, and some books (like Wisdom and Sirach) were left in the Old Latin.

misattributed.line: "Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ."
misattributed.truth: Genuine (Commentary on Isaiah, Prologue: "ignoratio Scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est"). Listed here because it is often doubted.

opinions.position: Early in life: a Christian should give up pagan classics for Scripture. After his dream he swore off secular books.
opinions.side_note: Side (early): against pagan learning. He later softened; see the next item.
opinions.quote: How can Horace go with the psalter, Virgil with the gospels, Cicero with the apostle?
opinions.location: section 29 (the dream follows in section 30), written 384
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today think great literature and faith mix well, so the early view is a minority one; some Christian parents and schools still limit secular reading.

opinions.position: Later in life: secular learning is a captive to be made useful. Christians may take the wisdom of pagan writers and put it to work for the faith, as Israel took a captive woman as a wife.
opinions.side_note: Side (later): for classical learning, used critically. Change of mind noted.
opinions.quote: Is it surprising that I too, admiring the fairness of her form and the grace of her eloquence, desire to make that secular wisdom which is my captive and my handmaid, a matron of the true Israel?
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: The mainstream view today among educated Christians.

opinions.position: Understanding Scripture is a skill that needs study and a teacher. It is the only art everyone thinks they can do without training, and amateurs tear it to pieces.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with Ambrose's praise of simple faith, and with modern debates about private interpretation.
opinions.quote: The art of interpreting the scriptures is the only one of which all men everywhere claim to be masters.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many Protestants value every believer reading and interpreting the Bible for themselves; Catholics, Orthodox and many scholars stress trained teachers and tradition. Good quiz claim: "You need real study before you can explain the Bible to anyone."

opinions.position: You cannot know Christ without knowing the Scriptures well; he urged friends to live among the books of the Bible and "know nothing else".
opinions.side_note: Own rendering of the Latin; the English line in Letter 53 section 10 says the same in NPNF wording.
opinions.quote: ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
opinions.translation: Own close rendering of the Latin: "ignoratio Scripturarum, ignoratio Christi est"
opinions.today: Split: many Christians hold that a simple believer who barely reads the Bible can know Christ deeply; others (and Jerome) say real faith needs real knowledge of Scripture.

opinions.position: As a young man he begged a friend to leave the city for the desert: the wilderness is where God is, and cities are a prison.
opinions.side_note: Side (early): for solitude. He changed his mind; see the next item.
opinions.quote: O wilderness, gladdened with God's special presence! What keeps you in the world, my brother, you who are above the world?
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Few people today think the city is spiritually worse than the country, though many feel nature brings them closer to God.

opinions.position: Later: a young monk should not live alone. He needs a community and a superior, to learn obedience and humility first; solitude only after long training.
opinions.side_note: Side (later): community before solitude. Change of mind from Letter 14.
opinions.quote: What then, you will say? Do I condemn a solitary life? By no means: in fact I have often commended it. But I wish to see the monastic schools turn out soldiers who have no fear of the rough training
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in modern terms: "Do you grow more by yourself or with others holding you to account?" Introverts and independents lean one way, community-minded people the other.

opinions.position: In 393: believers ought to visit the Holy Land and worship where the Lord's feet stood.
opinions.side_note: Side (earlier): for pilgrimage. Reversed two years later.
opinions.quote: it is still your duty as believers to worship on the spot where the Lord's feet once stood and to see for yourselves the still fresh traces of His
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many Christians value pilgrimage; many others see it as optional or touristic. Moderate split.

opinions.position: About 395: what matters is not having been to Jerusalem but living well; heaven is as open from Britain as from Jerusalem.
opinions.side_note: Side (later): against making pilgrimage important. Change of mind.
opinions.quote: What is praiseworthy is not to have been at Jerusalem but to have lived a good life while there.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would agree, so it is one-sided on its own; pairs usefully with the earlier letter.

opinions.position: If your family tries to hold you back from following Christ, go anyway, even stepping over your own father.
opinions.side_note: Side: calling over family, at its harshest. Written in his fiery youth.
opinions.quote: should your father prostrate himself on the threshold, trample him under foot and go your way. With dry eyes fly to the standard of the cross. In such cases cruelty is the only true affection.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today would recoil from the wording, but "follow your calling even if your family objects" genuinely splits people.

opinions.position: A Christian mother's endless weeping for a dead daughter is unbelief; grief that knows no limit insults the resurrection.
opinions.side_note: Side: against heavy mourning. He wept freely himself in the same letter and at Nepotian's death, so he was harder on others than on himself.
opinions.quote: Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears; for they know no limits, and bring you to the verge of death.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly one-sided against him: almost everyone today would call this cruel. Useful as a sparring line against Ambrose's gentler view.

opinions.position: A clergyman who gets rich through business is to be avoided like the plague. Those who serve Christ should not come out of it richer than they went in.
opinions.side_note: Side: against getting rich, especially for church workers.
opinions.quote: A clergyman who engages in business, and who rises from poverty to wealth, and from obscurity to a high position, avoid as you would the plague.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many are uneasy with wealthy pastors and prosperity preachers; others see nothing wrong with ministers earning well or running businesses.

opinions.position: Lavish churches of marble and gold miss the point: the believer's soul is Christ's true temple, and money should go to the poor and to choosing good ministers.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with Ambrose melting down church plate.
opinions.quote: The true temple of Christ is the believer's soul; adorn this, clothe it, offer gifts to it, welcome Christ in it.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some want beautiful churches as a gift to God and a witness; others think money for buildings should go to people.

opinions.position: Marriage is good, but mainly because it produces virgins; celibacy is the higher calling.
opinions.side_note: Side: celibacy above marriage, in its bluntest form.
opinions.quote: I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly one-sided against him today, including among most Christians; the Catholic and Orthodox view still ranks consecrated celibacy highly but would not phrase it this way.

opinions.position: Laughter and joking are for worldly people; someone serious about God should stay grave.
opinions.side_note: Side: against levity.
opinions.quote: Leave to worldlings the privileges of laughing and being laughed at. One who is in your position ought to be serious.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided against him today.

opinions.position: Young people, especially those vowed to God, should avoid wine as they would poison.
opinions.side_note: He allowed wine to children and the sick for health (Letter 107.8).
opinions.quote: I would begin by urging you and warning you as Christ's spouse to avoid wine as you would avoid poison. For wine is the first weapon used by demons against the young.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many Christians (Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Mormon-adjacent traditions) abstain; others drink freely in moderation.

opinions.position: A girl raised for God should not even know how instruments are played; let her learn psalms instead.
opinions.side_note: Side: against instrumental music in upbringing. Against Ambrose's love of hymn-singing.
opinions.quote: Let her be deaf to the sound of the organ, and not know even the uses of the pipe, the lyre, and the cithern.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided against him today (a few traditions, such as the Churches of Christ, still avoid instruments in worship).

opinions.position: He was glad to leave Rome's arena, circus and theatre to others.
opinions.side_note: Side: against public entertainments.
opinions.quote: Let Rome keep to itself its noise and bustle, let the cruel shows of the arena go on, let the crowd rave at the circus
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split in modern form: violent sport and entertainment divide people.

opinions.position: Some opinions deserve anger. He admits his indignation overpowers him and sees no need to hide it.
opinions.side_note: Side: for zealous anger in defence of truth.
opinions.quote: I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some admire passionate conviction; many think anger in argument is always a failure.

opinions.position: Severity in defending God's honour is not cruelty; he cites Phinehas, Elijah and Peter with Ananias.
opinions.side_note: Written about Vigilantius. Pairs against Martin's patience with Brictio.
opinions.quote: There is no cruelty in regard for God's honour.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly rejected today; most people think kindness should govern religious disagreement.

opinions.position: If someone thinks you have done wrong, they should tell you to your face, not talk about you behind your back.
opinions.side_note: Side: for open, direct correction.
opinions.quote: if I do wrong and you wish to correct me, accuse me openly of my fault: do not backbite me secretly.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Broadly agreed in principle; people split on whether they actually prefer being told directly.

opinions.position: Do not run others down, and do not listen to those who do.
opinions.side_note: Advice to a young priest.
opinions.quote: Beware also of a blabbing tongue and of itching ears. Neither detract from others nor listen to detractors.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Agreed in principle, broken in practice. One-sided as a bare claim; sharper as "I never listen when someone runs another person down."

opinions.position: He admired a student who would not simply accept his answers but pushed back, not to win but to find the answers to every objection.
opinions.side_note: Side: for questioning teachers. About Marcella, whom he treated as an equal in Scripture study.
opinions.quote: she never came to see me that she did not ask me some question concerning them, nor would she at once acquiesce in my explanations but on the contrary would dispute them; not, however, for argument's sake but to learn the answers
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today admire this; it splits only against a strong "trust your teachers" instinct.

opinions.topic: new: fighting to win an argument
opinions.position: In a debate you may use feints and say things you do not mean to beat your opponent; only when teaching must you be frank and open. Victory means the opponent is finished.
opinions.side_note: Relates to "lying": he distinguishes arguing to win from teaching. Against Augustine, who held that even useful untruths are wrong.
opinions.quote: One argues as one pleases, saying one thing while one means another.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some think winning an argument by any fair-seeming move is fine; many think you should only ever say what you believe. Quiz form: "In an argument, I'll use any point that wins, even one I'm not sure of."

opinions.position: A friendship that can end was never a true one; love cannot be bought.
opinions.side_note: Written to Rufinus, whom he later denounced in print for years. The irony is part of the story.
opinions.quote: Love is not to be purchased, and affection has no price. The friendship which can cease has never been real.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some believe true friends are for life; others think friendships naturally run their course and that is fine.

opinions.position: Nearly every strength of the body fades with age, but wisdom keeps growing; the old have more of it.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with his line to Augustine that "the tired ox treads with a firmer step".
opinions.quote: Almost all bodily excellences alter with age, and while wisdom alone increases all things else decay.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many cultures and older people agree; a youth-focused culture often doubts that age brings wisdom.

opinions.position: Teach a child with play, praise and friendly rivalry, not scolding. Make lessons pleasant so she does not come to hate learning, and do not let her learn habits she will have to unlearn.
opinions.side_note: A gentler side of Jerome, in a letter otherwise strict about the same child's upbringing.
opinions.quote: You must not scold her if she is slow to learn but must employ praise to excite her mind, so that she may be glad when she excels others and sorry when she is excelled by them.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Praise over scolding is mainstream; using competition (glad to beat others) splits parents and teachers.

opinions.position: Idleness invites temptation; always have work in hand. Even the apostles worked with their hands.
opinions.side_note: Pairs against Martin's monastery, where the older monks did no work but prayer.
opinions.quote: Always have some work on hand, that the devil may find you busy.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many agree ("idle hands"); many others today value rest and doing nothing as healthy. Genuine split.

opinions.position: Honouring the bodies and relics of martyrs is right; it is not worship of the creature but honour that passes to Christ.
opinions.side_note: Against Vigilantius, who called relic-venerators "ashmongers and idolaters".
opinions.quote: Still we honour the relics of the martyrs, that we may adore Him whose martyrs they are.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split along church lines: Catholics and Orthodox honour relics; most Protestants and secular people find it strange.

opinions.position: A bishop of a tiny town is equal to the bishop of Rome; wealth or a great city makes no one greater. Presbyters and bishops were originally the same office.
opinions.side_note: Written against deacons in Rome who put on airs above presbyters.
opinions.quote: Wherever there is a bishop, whether it be at Rome or at Engubium, whether it be at Constantinople or at Rhegium, whether it be at Alexandria or at Zoan, his dignity is one and his priesthood is one.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people like the egalitarian point; in church terms it splits Catholics (papal primacy) from Protestants and many Orthodox.

opinions.position: A grown woman vowed to God should not bathe at all: she should be ashamed to see herself undressed, and a deliberate squalor helps kill desire.
opinions.side_note: Extreme bodily asceticism. He allowed baths for small children.
opinions.quote: For myself, however, I wholly disapprove of baths for a virgin of full age.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Entirely one-sided against him today. Not a quiz statement, but a vivid, true fact for the reveal.

opinions.position: Later in life he warned against extreme fasting, which breaks weak bodies before holiness is built.
opinions.side_note: Contrast with his own desert extremes (Letter 22.7). Change of emphasis.
opinions.quote: I do not, however, lay on you as an obligation any extreme fasting or abnormal abstinence from food. Such practices soon break down weak constitutions
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most agree with moderation today.

opinions.position: Do not hope the devil (or anyone) will repent after death; life is won or lost here.
opinions.side_note: Side: against universal restoration, after he turned against Origen.
opinions.quote: Let us not wait for the repentance of the devil; for this is a vain anticipation and one that will drag us into the deep of hell. Life must be sought or lost here.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many today hope everyone is saved in the end; traditional Christians agree with Jerome.

opinions.position: Willing and striving are truly ours, but they fail unless God keeps helping.
opinions.side_note: Side: grace and effort together, against Pelagius.
opinions.quote: To will and to run are mine, but they will cease to be mine unless God brings me His continual aid.
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most Christians accept some version of this; secular people would put it all down to effort.

opinions.position: The fall of Rome broke his heart: he felt it as a personal grief, though he had left the city decades before.
opinions.side_note: Pairs against Augustine's City of God, which told Christians not to tie their hopes to Rome.
opinions.quote: My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken
opinions.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 6 (1893), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some people feel deep attachment to their nation or civilisation; others, including many Christians, say earthly nations should not hold our hearts.

sparring.over: Origen. Once his closest friend, Rufinus translated Origen's On First Principles and cited Jerome's earlier praise of Origen; Jerome answered with a three-book Apology and years of abuse. Rufinus hit back that Jerome had sworn off the classics and still quoted them.
sparring.source: Rufinus, Apology against Jerome; Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Books 1-3

sparring.over: Whether Paul's rebuke of Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2) was real or a staged "pious policy" (Augustine: Scripture can contain no useful lie); and whether to translate the Old Testament from Hebrew rather than the Greek Septuagint.
sparring.source: Jerome, Letters 102, 105 and 112 (Augustine's Letters 68, 72 and 75); Augustine, Letters 28, 40, 71 and 82

sparring.over: Jerome mocked Ambrose's book On the Holy Spirit as borrowed Greek feathers on an ungainly jackdaw, "flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty", without naming him.
sparring.source: Jerome's preface to Didymus On the Holy Spirit, quoted in Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2, sections 24-25

sparring.over: Origenism and church authority in Palestine: a four-year quarrel that amounted, in the NPNF editor's words, to "the practical excommunication of Jerome and his friends".
sparring.source: To Pammachius against John of Jerusalem

sparring.over: Whether virgins, widows and the married have equal merit, and whether fasting earns any reward. Jerome's reply was so fierce that his friends in Rome tried to keep it from circulating.
Whether Mary had other children after Jesus.
sparring.source: The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary (Against Helvidius)

sparring.over: Relics, night vigils at martyrs' shrines and monks; Jerome called him "Dormitantius".
Whether a person can live without sin by his own effort.
sparring.source: Letter 133 (to Ctesiphon); Dialogue against the Pelagians

sparring.over: His attacks on worldly clergy and his influence over aristocratic women, after which he left Rome in 385.

figures.name: Martin of Tours
figures.dates: born c. 316 (some scholars say c. 336) at Savaria in Pannonia (Szombathely, Hungary); bishop of Tours from c. 371; died 8 November 397 at Candes
figures.places: Savaria; Pavia (childhood); the Roman army in Gaul (Amiens); Poitiers with Hilary; Illyricum; Milan; the island of Gallinaria; Ligugé; Tours and his monastery at Marmoutier; the court of Maximus at Trier; Candes (death)
figures.role: Soldier turned monk; founder of the first monasteries in Gaul (Ligugé, Marmoutier); bishop of Tours; wonder-worker, destroyer of pagan shrines, and opponent of executing heretics
figures.status_note: Saint in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Anglican churches; one of the first saints honoured in the West who was not a martyr; patron of France, soldiers and the poor (feast 11 November, Martinmas). Cautions: (1) he wrote nothing that survives. Every word of his comes through Sulpicius Severus, a devoted disciple who met him, wrote his Life while Martin was alive, and fills it with miracles; the Dialogues put Martin's stories in the mouths of friends (Gallus, Postumianus). His sayings are well attested for the period, but they are reports, not writings. (2) Sulpicius's chronology of his army years is muddled, and some historians think he served much longer than Sulpicius says. (3) He led crowds to demolish pagan temples and cut down sacred trees, which modern readers may find troubling next to his gentleness and his stand against executing heretics.
figures.hook: A young cavalry guard cut his army cloak in half with his sword for a freezing beggar at Amiens, and later told the emperor on the eve of battle, "I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight."

stories.story: In a hard winter at the gate of Amiens, a naked beggar was pleading with passers-by and everyone ignored him. Martin, a young soldier who had already given away his other clothes, drew his sword, cut his military cloak in two and gave the beggar half. Some bystanders laughed at how he looked. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak and saying to the angels: "Martin, who is still but a catechumen, clothed me with this robe."
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin, chapter 3

stories.story: Before a battle with the Germans, when the emperor Julian was handing out a bonus to his troops, Martin asked to leave the army: "I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight." Accused of cowardice, he offered to stand unarmed in front of the battle line the next day, protected only by the sign of the cross. The enemy sued for peace before the battle could happen.
stories.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 4

stories.story: Crossing the Alps he was caught by robbers. One raised an axe over his head; another stopped the blow. Tied up and led away, he was asked by his guard whether he was afraid. He said he had never felt so safe, because God's mercy was with him in trials, and he preached to the robber, who became a Christian and later told the story himself.
stories.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 5

stories.story: The people of Tours wanted him as bishop but knew he would not leave his monastery, so a citizen tricked him out by pretending his wife was sick. Some bishops objected that he was "despicable in countenance, that his clothing was mean, and his hair disgusting"; the people laughed at them and made him bishop anyway. He kept living like a monk, in a wooden cell at Marmoutier outside the city.
stories.source: Life of St Martin, chapters 9-10

stories.story: At a banquet the usurper-emperor Maximus had the cup passed first to Martin, expecting to receive it back from his hand. Martin drank and handed it to his own priest, "thinking no one worthier". The whole court admired it.
stories.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 20

stories.story: At Trier, bishops were pressing Maximus to hunt down the followers of the executed heretic Priscillian. To save men already condemned and to stop troops being sent into Spain, Martin agreed for one day to take communion with those bishops. On the road home he sat alone in the woods tormented by it; he said afterwards that his power to heal had weakened, and for the remaining sixteen years of his life he never attended another synod.
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues, Book 3 (New Advent division), chapters 11-13

stories.story: His own pupil Brictio, a priest who had grown rich keeping horses and buying slaves, stormed in and screamed abuse at him, calling him a senile old soldier full of superstitions. Martin answered him calmly, forgave him when he came back in tears, and refused for years to remove him from the priesthood, saying: "If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio." Brictio later succeeded him as bishop of Tours.
stories.source: Dialogues, Book 3 (New Advent division), chapter 15

stories.story: Old and ill, he travelled to Candes to reconcile its quarrelling clergy and died there, lying on sackcloth and ashes. When his disciples begged to put straw under him he said: "It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example."
stories.source: Sulpicius Severus, Letter 3 (to Bassula)

temperament.trait: Unshakably calm (as his disciple saw him)
temperament.evidence: "No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance".

temperament.trait: Patient under insult, even from his own clergy
temperament.evidence: "He displayed indeed such marvelous patience in the endurance of injuries, that even when he was chief priest, he allowed himself to be wronged by the lowest clerics with impunity".
Sulpicius on his first visit: "He went so far as in person to present me with water to wash my hands, and at eventide he himself washed my feet".
Before Maximus "he commanded rather than entreated him", and he refused the emperor's table because Maximus had "deprived one of his kingdom, and the other of his life".
"Frequently, too, he used to weep for the sins of those who showed themselves his revilers".
Hostile bishops said "that he was a man despicable in countenance, that his clothing was mean, and his hair disgusting."

genuine_lines.quote: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin (his words to the emperor Julian)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio.
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues (a saying he often repeated)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: The Lord Jesus did not predict that he would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon his head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless he appears with that appearance and form in which he suffered, and openly displaying the marks of his wounds upon the cross.
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin (to the devil disguised as Christ)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: 'See,' says he, 'she has fulfilled the precept of the Gospel: she had two coats, and one of them she has given to him who had none: thus, therefore, you ought also to do.'
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues (on seeing a newly shorn sheep)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: O Lord, if I am still necessary to your people, I do not shrink from toil: your will be done.
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Letter 3 (his prayer on his deathbed, as reported)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

genuine_lines.quote: Look at Adam, cast out of Paradise, how he feeds his swine in a garment of skin; but let us, laying aside that old Adam, who still remains in that man, rather put on the new Adam.
genuine_lines.work: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues (on seeing a half-naked swineherd)
genuine_lines.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent

misattributed.line: Martin hid among geese to avoid being made bishop, and their honking gave him away (the origin of the Martinmas goose).
misattributed.truth: A later folk legend. Sulpicius says a citizen named Ruricius tricked him out of his monastery by pretending his wife was ill (Life, chapter 9).

misattributed.line: He gave only half his cloak because the other half belonged to the Roman army.
misattributed.truth: A modern explanation, not in Sulpicius, who says simply that he had nothing else left to give, having already given away his other clothes (Life, chapter 3).

None survive. A short "Confession of Faith on the Trinity" once circulated under his name but is not accepted as his; everything reliable comes through Sulpicius Severus (and later Paulinus of Périgueux and Gregory of Tours, who depend on Sulpicius).

opinions.position: A Christian may not fight. He left the army on the eve of battle and offered to face the enemy unarmed to prove it was not cowardice.
opinions.side_note: Side: against Christians fighting. Against Ambrose, who called courage in war "full of justice".
opinions.quote: Hitherto I have served you as a soldier: allow me now to become a soldier to God: let the man who is to serve you receive your donative: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: most people, Christians included, think serving in the military can be right; pacifists and conscientious objectors side with Martin. A classic, clean quiz claim.

opinions.position: When a pagan attacked him with a sword, he threw back his cloak and offered his bare neck rather than defend himself.
opinions.side_note: Practice, recorded by Sulpicius. Pairs with Ambrose's view that a Christian may not strike back at an armed robber.
opinions.quote: And when one of them, bolder than the rest, made an attack upon him with a drawn sword, Martin, throwing back his cloak, offered his bare neck to the assassin.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Almost everyone today would defend themselves; only strict pacifists would not. One-sided, but striking in a reveal.

opinions.position: Heretics should not be put to death. Being condemned by bishops and put out of the churches is punishment enough, and a secular ruler has no business judging a church case.
opinions.side_note: Side: against the state punishing religious error. Ambrose took the same line in the Priscillian affair (Letter 24.12).
opinions.quote: He maintained that it was quite sufficient punishment that, having been declared heretics by a sentence of the bishops, they should have been expelled from the churches; and that it was, besides, a foul and unheard-of indignity, that a secular ruler should be judge in an ecclesiastical cause.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Near-unanimous agreement today that no one should be punished by the state for religious beliefs; one-sided now, but it was brave then.

opinions.position: Pagan temples and sacred trees had no holiness and should be torn down and replaced with churches; he led crowds to do it, though he often persuaded the villagers to pull down their own temples.
opinions.side_note: Practice, recorded by Sulpicius. Sits uneasily beside his opposition to executing heretics.
opinions.quote: Martin carefully instructed them that there was nothing sacred in the trunk of a tree, and urged them rather to honor God whom he himself served.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Rejected by most people today, who value religious freedom and heritage. One-sided now; a truth readers should know.

opinions.position: Past sins are wiped out by a changed life, and even those who had fallen away after baptism should be taken back. He told the devil himself that if he repented, Martin would promise him Christ's mercy.
opinions.side_note: Side: for second chances, at its widest (even the devil). Relates to universal-salvation.
opinions.quote: If you, yourself, wretched being, would but desist from attacking mankind, and even, at this period, when the day of judgment is at hand, would only repent of your deeds, I, with a true confidence in the Lord, would promise you the mercy of Christ.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people agree anyone who truly changes deserves another chance; many draw the line at the worst offenders. Against Jerome's "Let us not wait for the repentance of the devil".

opinions.topic: new: bearing with people who wrong you
opinions.position: Put up with those who insult and wrong you, as Christ put up with Judas. He would not even discipline his abusive priest, so that no one could think he was taking revenge.
opinions.side_note: Relates to correction and anger. Against Jerome's zeal.
opinions.quote: Martin could not be induced to remove him from the presbyterate, lest he should be suspected of revenging the injury done to himself, while he often repeated this saying: 'If Christ bore with Judas, why should not I bear with Brictio.'
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many admire such patience; many others (especially after church abuse scandals) say leaders must remove wrongdoers, whatever it looks like.

opinions.position: Selling everything and giving it to the poor is what the Gospel asks; he held up Paulinus of Nola, who did so, as almost the only man of his time who had fully obeyed it.
opinions.side_note: Side: for radical renunciation.
opinions.quote: Martin declared of him that, by parting with his great possessions and following Christ, as he did, he showed himself almost the only one who in these times had fully obeyed the precepts of the Gospel.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people, including most Christians, think you can follow Jesus without giving away everything; a minority admire and aim at it.

opinions.position: Do not keep money back for your own future needs. Given a large gift of silver, he sent it all to ransom captives, and when his hungry, ragged monks asked him to keep some, he said the Church should feed and clothe them.
opinions.side_note: Relates to wealth. A good everyday question about saving versus giving.
opinions.quote: 'Let the church both feed and clothe us, as long as we do not appear to have provided, in any way, for our own wants.'
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Strongly split: most people think it is prudent and responsible to save; some Christians practise giving away rather than saving, trusting God to provide.

opinions.position: Marriage is good and not to be despised, but virginity is higher. Those who equate marriage with fornication are badly wrong, and so are those who put marriage on a level with virginity.
opinions.side_note: Side: celibacy above marriage, but marriage honourable. His picture of a meadow: grazed grass (marriage), ground rooted up by pigs (fornication), untouched flowers (virginity).
opinions.quote: Thus, then, those who set marriage side by side with fornication grievously err; and those who think that marriage is to be placed on an equal footing with virginity are utterly wretched and foolish.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today, including most Protestants, reject ranking celibacy above marriage; Catholic and Orthodox teaching still honours consecrated celibacy as a higher calling.

opinions.position: Be suspicious of dazzling spiritual experiences. When the devil appeared to him as Christ in a crown and royal robes, Martin refused to believe: the real Christ would come with the wounds of the cross.
opinions.side_note: Side: sceptical of visions and signs that flatter.
opinions.quote: I will not believe that Christ has come, unless he appears with that appearance and form in which he suffered, and openly displaying the marks of his wounds upon the cross.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: many Christians are open to visions and signs; others are sceptical of them.

opinions.position: Do not go along with a popular shrine just because everyone venerates it. He asked for the martyr's name and date, found no reliable tradition, and had the altar removed when it proved to belong to an executed robber.
opinions.side_note: Relates to questioning. Pairs against Jerome's defence of relics (Martin himself honoured true martyrs).
opinions.quote: But Martin, not inclined to give a hasty belief to things uncertain, often asked from those who were his elders, whether among the presbyters or clerics, that the name of the martyr, or the time when he suffered, should be made known to him.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some people trust long-standing popular devotion; others want evidence before they believe a claim, even a pious one.

opinions.position: Holding office cost him spiritually: he said his power was greater as a monk than as a bishop.
opinions.side_note: Side: reluctant office-holder (he was tricked into it).
opinions.quote: Martin was accustomed to say to you, that such an abundance of power was by no means granted him while he was a bishop, as he remembered to have possessed before he obtained that office.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many people feel leadership and responsibility wear them down; others find purpose in it. Moderate split.

opinions.position: He once went against his conscience, taking communion with bishops he condemned, to save men from execution. He thought it was the only way out, grieved over it for the rest of his life, and never did it again.
opinions.side_note: A rare case of a Father recorded as choosing "dirty hands" and regretting it.
opinions.quote: Martin took part in the communion of that day, judging it better to yield for the moment, than to disregard the safety of those over whose heads a sword was hanging.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Genuinely split: some say you must never compromise your principles; others say saving lives justifies it. Strong quiz claim: "I'd go against my conscience if it saved someone's life."

opinions.position: Do not defer to rulers because of their rank: he refused a usurper's dinners and, when he did attend, passed the emperor's cup to his own priest rather than back to the emperor.
opinions.side_note: Pairs with Ambrose barring Theodosius.
opinions.quote: But Martin, when he had drunk, handed the goblet to his own presbyter, as thinking no one worthier to drink next to himself
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people admire this in principle; split on whether one should show special respect to political leaders.

opinions.position: Men and women vowed to God should live apart. When a soldier-turned-monk wanted his wife to live with him in the monastery, Martin compared it to women standing in the battle line.
opinions.side_note: Uncomfortable today; recorded by a friend who says these were Martin's "very words".
opinions.quote: 'Let not a woman enter the camp of men, but let the line of soldiers remain separate, and let the females, dwelling in their own tent, be remote from that of men.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Mostly rejected today, though some religious communities (and some conservative Christians, e.g. the "Billy Graham rule") keep strict separation between the sexes.

opinions.position: Even as bishop he withdrew to a remote cell outside the city because crowds of visitors disturbed him; he praised a woman hermit for refusing to see even him.
opinions.side_note: Side: for solitude, within a community of monks.
opinions.quote: he established a monastery for himself about two miles outside the city. This spot was so secret and retired that he enjoyed in it the solitude of a hermit.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split between people who recharge alone and people who thrive in company.

opinions.position: When a woman hermit refused to let even him visit, he took no offence and went away praising her.
opinions.side_note: About not taking rejection personally.
opinions.quote: O blessed Martin, who did not regard that repulse as being any insult to himself, but, extolling with exultant heart her excellence, rejoiced in an example only too rare in that locality!
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most would say they should not take it personally; many would admit they would.

opinions.position: A Christian should die in penance, on ashes, and not ask for comfort even at the end.
opinions.side_note: Side: strict asceticism to the last.
opinions.quote: It is not fitting that a Christian should die except among ashes; and I have sinned if I leave you a different example.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: One-sided against him today; most want comfort at the end of life.

opinions.position: Animals deserve pity: he called off hunting dogs to let a hunted hare escape, and read lessons from sheep and swine.
opinions.side_note: Practice and sayings, recorded by friends who were there.
opinions.quote: Now the blessed man pitied the danger of the creature with pious feelings, and commanded the dogs to give up following it, and to permit it to get safe away.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split on hunting: many see nothing wrong with it; many others share his pity for the hunted animal.

opinions.position: Making peace between quarrelling people is worth the last of your strength; he spent his final journey reconciling a divided church.
opinions.side_note: Recorded by Sulpicius from those present.
opinions.quote: as the clerics of that church were at variance among themselves, Martin, wishing to restore peace, although he well knew that the end of his own days was at hand, yet he did not shrink from undertaking the journey, with such an object in view.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Agreed in principle; people split on whether to step into other people's quarrels.

opinions.position: Rank should not decide who serves whom: as a young officer with one servant, he often waited on the servant, cleaning his boots and serving him at meals.
opinions.side_note: Practice, recorded by Sulpicius.
opinions.quote: he drew off his [servant's] boots and cleaned them with his own hand; while they took their meals together, the real master, however, generally acting the part of servant.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most admire it; people split on whether bosses should ever do the lowliest work themselves.

opinions.position: In his monastery no craft was practised except copying books, done by the young; the older monks did nothing but pray. Nothing was bought or sold, and no one owned anything.
opinions.side_note: The rule of Marmoutier as Sulpicius describes it. Against Jerome's "Always have some work on hand".
opinions.quote: No art was practiced there, except that of transcribers, and even this was assigned to the brethren of younger years, while the elders spent their time in prayer.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Most people today value work and productivity; a contemplative minority would agree prayer can be a whole life's work.

opinions.position: In real danger a believer can feel safer than ever, because God's mercy is nearest in trials.
opinions.side_note: His answer to the robber holding him prisoner.
opinions.quote: Then indeed Martin most courageously replied that he never before had felt so safe, because he knew that the mercy of the Lord would be especially present with him in the midst of trials.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Many believers describe exactly this; many others would say fear is natural and honest.

opinions.position: At ten he went to the church to become a catechumen against his pagan parents' wishes; his father later had him arrested and forced into the army.
opinions.side_note: Side: calling over family. Practice, recorded by Sulpicius.
opinions.quote: For, when he was of the age of ten years, he betook himself, against the wish of his parents, to the Church, and begged that he might become a catechumen.
opinions.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, 2nd series, vol. 11 (1894), as revised for New Advent
opinions.today: Split: some say follow conscience even as a child; many say children should follow their parents.

sparring.with: Ithacius of Ossonuba and the Ithacian bishops
sparring.over: The prosecution and execution of Priscillian and the hunt for his followers. Martin urged that no blood be shed and refused communion with the accusers; Ithacius even accused Martin of heresy.
sparring.source: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2, chapter 50; Dialogues, Book 3 (New Advent division), chapters 11-13

sparring.over: Martin refused his table because he had overthrown one emperor and killed another; later pleaded against sending tribunes to Spain to kill heretics.
sparring.source: Life of St Martin, chapter 20; Dialogues, Book 3, chapters 11-13

sparring.over: Arianism: Auxentius persecuted Martin and drove him out of Milan, years before Ambrose's own clash with the same man.

sparring.with: Brictio (Brice), his own priest and later successor
sparring.over: Brictio's wealth, horses and slaves; Brictio called Martin a senile ex-soldier full of superstitions.

sparring.with: Defensor and other bishops at his election
sparring.over: They said he was too shabby and contemptible to be a bishop.
